extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners evaluating subject-matter eligibility for life sciences claims
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the USPTO Interim Eligibility Guidance (IEG) to life-science example claims (diagnostics, treatments, and nature-based product formulations) using the Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheets to determine patent-eligibility and to draft rejections when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the broadest reasonable interpretation affects the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the broadest reasonable interpretation when construing claim language for the subject-matter-eligibility analysis; BRI can affect whether a claim is seen as directed to a judicial exception or to additional patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify judicial exceptions in Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: How to identify judicial exceptions in Step 2A (e.g., laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Step 2A analysis to determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception. The July 2015 Update graphic and the case law chart available on the website may be used as guides for identifying abstract ideas and other exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additional elements in Step 2B, particularly combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: How to evaluate additional claim elements in Step 2B to determine if they amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception, with particular attention to combinations of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the additional elements, alone or in combination, integrate the exception into a practical application or otherwise add significantly more than the judicial exception itself. Consider whether any claimed combination produces a new/markedly different result or merely applies routine, conventional techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfy burden to make a prima facie case of ineligibility when writing a rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: How to write a rejection that satisfies your burden to make a prima facie case of ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection must explain why the claim is directed to a judicial exception (per Step 2A) and why the additional elements do not add significantly more (per Step 2B). Use the worksheets, claim construction, and appropriate case law to build the prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheets (generic and Nature-Based Products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which worksheet to use: generic Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheet vs Nature-Based Products Subject Matter Eligibility Worksheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze claims using the appropriate worksheet: use the generic worksheet for general life-science claims (e.g., diagnostics/treatments) and the Nature-Based Products worksheet for claims reciting nature-based products and mixtures. Worksheets structure the Step 2A/2B analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze examples under the 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility (IEG)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examples should be analyzed under the 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility (IEG).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the issued examples as illustrative only and interpret them based on the fact patterns set forth in the workshop materials. Other fact patterns may have different eligibility outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope for workshop exercises (do not address other patentability requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: For workshop purposes, other patentability requirements under §§ 102, 103, 112 and 101 (utility, inventorship, double patenting) and non-statutory double patenting need not be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the exercise exclusively on subject-matter-eligibility analysis (IEG Steps 2A/2B). Do not conflate novelty, obviousness, written description, or other procedural requirements with the eligibility determination for the workshop examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use July 2015 Update Quick Reference Sheet graphic and case law chart as identification aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the July 2015 Update graphic and the case law chart available on the website as guides for identifying abstract ideas and other judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These reference materials serve as tools to map claim features to categories of judicial exceptions and relevant precedent during the Step 2A analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether claimed detection/diagnostic methods are routine and conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify when claim steps recite routine and conventional methods (e.g., physical biopsies, immunoassays) and the implications for Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'discloses detecting JUL-1 by routine and conventional methods such as (i) physical biopsies of skin, hair or nails, or (ii) immunoassays ... contacting the sample with an antibody ... and then binding between the antibody and the protein is detected using a laboratory technique such as fluoroscopy.' If elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional at the time of filing, they may not supply the 'significantly more' required in Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether nature-based product claims retain naturally occurring characteristics or are materially altered
rubrics_metrics.description: For nature-based products and mixtures, evaluate whether the claimed formulation retains the naturally occurring product's characteristics (e.g., texiol's sweetness and bitter aftertaste) or results in changed/markedly different properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Nature-Based Products Worksheet to analyze: examples include formulations that 'retain the naturally occurring texiol’s sweetness and bitter aftertaste' versus modifications (e.g., addition of Compound N that neutralizes bitter aftertaste, solid gel formulations with pectin, granulated texiol with specified particle size distributions, controlled release formulations via encapsulation) that may produce different characteristics (improved organoleptic properties, consistent dissolution rates, prolonged sweetness) and thus could impact eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider manufacturing/process features and specified parameters as potential inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether claimed manufacturing/process features (e.g., granulation to achieve X10/X90 particle sizes, crystallization controls, encapsulation for controlled release, addition of pectin) produce tangible, practical improvements beyond a natural product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Granular texiol having a particle size of X10 of 80 microns and X90 of 300 microns is preferred, because this particle size distribution results in a greatly increased (and consistent) dissolution rate ...' Such specific parameters and processing steps may support a finding of 'significantly more' if they produce new/markedly different properties as compared to the naturally occurring material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate source and nature of biological materials (naturally occurring vs non-naturally occurring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claimed biological materials are naturally occurring, isolated, or non-naturally occurring (e.g., naturally occurring anti-JUL-1 antibodies vs porcine or monoclonal antibodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the text: anti-JUL-1 antibodies that may be naturally occurring (isolated from a patient), non-naturally occurring (porcine anti-JUL-1 antibody created by injecting pigs), or a specific monoclonal antibody 'mAb-D33' created by applicant. Consider whether the material as claimed is merely a naturally occurring product or has been modified/isolated in a way that confers new characteristics or uses; also consider whether prior art use and routine application bear on whether the claimed material contributes 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether claimed treatment steps reflect unconventional clinical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether claimed therapeutic steps (e.g., administering topical vitamin D to julitis patients) reflect non-routine, non-conventional treatment that may supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Applicant has successfully treated julitis patients ... with topical vitamin D. Prior to applicant’s invention ... vitamin D was commonly used as an oral supplement ... but doctors were not commonly or routinely administering topical vitamin D to patients with julitis.' If the claimed treatment deviates from conventional practice and produces a demonstrable therapeutic effect, that may weigh in favor of eligibility under Step 2B.
